title: Tenant isolation at the database boundary and the policies it depends on

threat_model.actor: A legitimate user of one tenant, or any code path that reaches the database with a role or a session setting other than the one the isolation model assumes
threat_model.asset: Row-level separation between tenants, and the correctness of every aggregate, export, and background job derived from it
threat_model.trust_boundary: The tenant the request belongs to and the rows the executed statement is actually able to touch
threat_model.failure_mode: A statement omits the tenant predicate while the policy that was supposed to supply it does not apply to the connecting role, is not forced, or was never given its setting
threat_model.impact: Rows belonging to other tenants are read, aggregated, exported, or written, frequently through a reporting or background path rather than the primary request path

required_evidence: Rows belonging to different tenants, owners, or organisations share a table
At least one statement relies on something other than its own predicate to stay within one tenant

signals: A policy is enabled but not forced, while the application connects with the table's owning role
The policy reads a runtime setting that some code paths never set
The setting is applied for the session rather than for the transaction, so it survives on a pooled connection
A privileged or definer-rights function reads the table on behalf of the caller and applies no predicate of its own
More than one pool or role reaches the same tables, and only one of them enforces isolation
Reporting, analytics, migration, or admin paths use a separate connection with wider rights
A connection is returned to the pool without resetting the state a previous request set on it
A default scope supplies the tenant predicate and an escape hatch bypasses it
A raw query helper is used where the scoped API would have added the predicate
An association or eager-load traverses to rows the root scope never constrained
The repository's migrations and the live schema can disagree about which policies exist
A later migration replaces or drops a policy without restoring it
A new table is added without the isolation the other tables received
A reporting path borrows a pool whose role bypasses the row policy and carries no tenant predicate
A migration enables row level security without forcing it while the runtime role owns the table

boundary.subject: the tenant the executing statement belongs to
boundary.object: the rows the statement can read or write in a shared table
boundary.invariant: Every statement against a shared table is constrained to one tenant, either by its own predicate or by a policy that demonstrably applies to the connecting role with its setting bound for that transaction

examples: Item or list query without a tenant predicate
Join reaching a table the root scope never constrained
Update or delete matched by primary key alone
Insert whose tenant column comes from the request
Dashboard count over a shared table
Stored procedure invoked on behalf of a caller
Queue worker processing rows in bulk
Session setting left on a pooled connection
Role assumed for a maintenance path

signals: List every statement against shared tables and mark which carry a tenant predicate and which rely on a policy
Identify every role and pool that reaches those tables, including reporting, migration, and admin paths
Trace how the runtime setting a policy reads is established, and find the paths that never establish it
State the isolation mechanism per table and confirm it applies to the connecting role rather than only to some roles
Decide whether the setting is bound per transaction or per session, and what a pooled connection therefore inherits
Compare the policies the migrations create with the policies the deployed database actually holds
Establish which tables hold rows for more than one tenant and which of them have no policy at all
Check whether privileged routines, views, and materialised aggregates carry the predicate their callers assume
Against a local database seeded with two synthetic tenants, run each path and record which rows it returns
Borrow and release a pooled connection across two synthetic tenants and record what state the second request inherits

steps: Confirm explicit authorization and use a local database seeded with two synthetic tenants and no real customer data
Run the owning tenant's request first and record the rows returned, so a later difference is attributable to the boundary
Repeat every path — item, list, aggregate, export, and background — and record the rows each returns for the other tenant
Connect with each role the application uses and observe whether the policy applies to it
Record the role, the setting, the policy definition, and the statement text without mutating any shared environment

false_positive_filters: The statement carries its own tenant predicate, so the policy is defence in depth rather than the only control
The policy is forced and the connecting role neither owns the table nor holds a bypass attribute, evidenced from the schema rather than assumed
The setting the policy reads is bound per transaction on every path that reaches the table
The table holds no rows for more than one tenant, so the missing predicate has no isolation consequence
The path is a maintenance or migration tool that no request can reach, and its credentials are not available to the application
Separate databases or schemas per tenant make a shared-table predicate unnecessary, evidenced by the connection routing

required_evidence: The statement without a predicate, the role it executes as, and the policy that was supposed to constrain it
A reachable path from a caller of one tenant to that statement
A two-tenant reproduction on a local database showing which rows were returned or written
The defective invariant stated as a predicate, role, or setting failure, with the concrete isolation impact
refutation_tests: Read the policy definition and the connecting role together, since enabling a policy does not bind the owner unless it is forced
Check whether the setting is bound per transaction before concluding a pooled connection carries state across requests
Look for the predicate in a view, a default scope, or a wrapper the statement passes through
Confirm the table actually holds more than one tenant's rows before asserting cross-tenant impact

root_causes: A policy is enabled but not forced while the application connects as the table owner, which is exempt from it
A second pool or role reaches the same tables without the isolation the primary path relies on
The runtime setting a policy reads is never established on some paths, so the policy evaluates against nothing
The setting is session-scoped and survives on a pooled connection into the next request
Reporting and background paths omit the predicate because the primary path appears to be protected
Migrations and the deployed schema drift, so the policy in the repository is not the policy in force

variant_strategy.result_contract: EXACT | VARIANT | REFUTED | BLOCKED; exact and variant matches remain hypotheses until verified

remediation.canonical_invariant: Force the row policy, connect with a role it binds, bind its setting per transaction on every path, and keep the tenant predicate in the statement as defence in depth
patterns: Force row level security so the owning role is subject to the policy, and give the application a separate non-owning role
Bind the tenant setting as a parameter, scoped to the transaction, so nothing survives on a pooled connection
Route reporting, export, and background work through the same role and the same enforcement as the request path
Keep an explicit tenant predicate in each statement, so the policy is a second layer rather than the only one
Give security-definer routines their own predicate rather than inheriting the caller's assumptions
Assert the deployed policy set in a test that reads the live schema, so migration drift fails visibly

assertions: The vulnerable reporting path aggregates rows across tenants because it borrows a role that bypasses the policy and carries no predicate
The vulnerable primary path interpolates the tenant into a session-scoped setting that survives on the pooled connection
The remediated database uses one enforcing role, binds the setting per transaction, and repeats the predicate, while still returning the owning tenant's rows
The vulnerable repository runs predicate-free statements under a policy that is enabled but not forced, with the runtime role owning the table
The compensated repository runs the same predicate-free statements safely because the policy is forced and the runtime role is not the owner

calibration.notes: This pack has not completed a reproducible benchmark run and makes no precision or recall claim.

limitations: Policy semantics differ between database engines, so conclusions about forcing, ownership, and bypass do not transfer between them
The deployed schema is the authority and may differ from the migrations in the repository, which code review alone cannot settle
Connection pooling and role assignment are usually configured outside the repository and decide much of the real behaviour
The synthetic fixtures demonstrate the enforcement contract, not the policy set of any particular production database
